speeches.1: H OW now gallants, what iſt? what iſt? If ſome had had the wit to doe ſo in time, they might haue ſau'd the hang-man a labour. But come boy, furniſh us with ſtooles. And you were the Epilogue to ſir— Prethee where is he? Then he muſt lay his triall upon God and good wits But why doth he call his play The Ile of Gulls? it begets much expectation. Out a queſtion he hath promiſed thee ſome fee, thou pleadeſt ſo hard for him, but and he be a right Poet he will never performe it. But what method obſerues he in his Play, iſt any thing Criticall? Are Lawyers fees, and Citizens wiues laid open in it? I loue to heare vice anatomizd, and abuſe let blood in the maſter vaine, is there any great mans life charactred in't? All that's nothing to mee, and there bee not Worme-wood water and Copperes in't, Ile not like it, ſhould Apollo write it, and Roſius himſelfe act it. Looke to't, if there be not gall in't, it ſhall not paſſe. Enemies? nays foote then there's ſome hope in his play, for Envie never workes but againſt deſert and merit. If he be envied theres ſome worth in him, and ile ſee out his play for that onely.
speeches.2: The Ile of Guls. A play by the name, but come ſhals quarter our ſelues? Fie be not incivill: doſt heare youth, prethee what's he that diſcovered your new found Land, the Ile of Guls? what is he? And where ſit his friends? hath he not a prepared company of gallants, to applaud his jeſts, and grace out his play? Fie upon thee, thou art too too criticall: is there any good baudry in't, jeſts of an ell deepe, and a fathome broad, good cuckol ding, may a couple of young-ſetters-up learne to doe well in't? Giue me a Scene of venery, that will make a mans ſpirits ſtand on their tiptoes, and die his blood in a deepe ſcarlet, like your Ovids Ars Amandi, there flowes the true Spring-head of Poetry, and the very Chriſtall fount of Parnaſſus. Chaſt eares? now deafeneſſe light upon them, what ſhould chaſt eares doe at a play? Fie upon't, more fuſtian; I had rather heare two good baudy jeſts, then a whole play of ſuch teare-cat thunder-claps. If it be not baudy, tis impoſſible to paſſe: Faith and Ile ſee an act or two out, but I tell you afore-hand I cannot ſee it out. Fore God I lay in bed till paſt three a clock, ſlept out my din ner, and my ſtomacke will toule to ſupper afore fiue, therefore you muſt pardon me. Well, Ile ſit out the play, an't bee but to avoyd that ſheepiſh imputation, but ſee it be baudy, or by this light I and all my friends will hiſſe.
speeches.3: The Ile of Guls, what ſhould that be? A ſtranger? the better welcome: comes hee Eaſt-ward, Weſt-ward, or North-ward hoe? The beſt in grace doe, and but for that, ſome that I know, had never had their grace in Poetry till this day. Tis ſtrange now, I am of neither a both your opinions, I like neither rayling nor baudry: no, giue me a ſtately pend hiſtorie, as thus: The rugged winds, with rude and ragged ruffes, &c. If it bee both criticall and baudy, if it bee not high written, both your Poet and the houſe too, looſe a friend of me. Not ſee it out? your reaſon. Why doeſt thinke thy audience like a flock of ſheepe, that one cannot leape over a hedge, but all the reſt will follow? they haue more of reaſon in them then ſo.
Pardon mee ſir, my office is to ſpeake a Prologue, not to provide you ſtooles. A meere ſtranger ſir. None of the three wayes I aſſure you. Not on his knees in a comer to Apollo, praying that his play may hold in a good hand at Paſſage, nor on the ſtage amongſt gal lants, preparing a beſpoke Plaudite; but cloſe in his ſtudy writing hard, to get him a handſome ſuite againſt Summer. None I proteſt ▪ Do Poets uſe to beſpeake their Auditory? Then muſt our Author looké for a certaine diſgrace, for he is altogether unfurniſht of ſuch a friendly audience. Not out of any dogged diſpoſition, nor that it figures any certaine ſtate, or private government: farre bee that ſuppoſition from the thought of any indifferent Auditor: and the argument being a little ſtring or • ivolet, drawen from the full ſtraine of the right worthy Gentleman Sir Phillip Sydnies well knowne Arca dia, confirmes it: only a Duke, to make triall of certaine experi ments, retires with his retinue into a nameleſſe deſert. Now as well for faſhion ſake, as that all thoſe which haue to doe in that de ſert, are guld in the reach of their hopes; therefore he cals it, (and as he preſumes, not improperly) The Ile of Gulls. None I proteſt ſir, only in the perſon of Dametas, he ex preſſes to the life the monſtrous and deformed ſhape of vice, aſwell to beget a loathing of abuſe, as that his villany may giue the greater luſter to the vertuous diſpoſitions of true-borne gentility. Chaſt eares would never endure it fir. Alas Gentlemen, bow iſt poſſible to content you? you wil haue rayling, and invectiues, which our Author neither dares, nor affects: you baudy and ſcurrill jeſts, which neither becomes his modeſty to write, nor the eare of a generous Auditory to heare: you muſt haue ſwelling compariſons, and • um • aſt Epithites, which are as fit for the body of a Com • edy ▪ as Her •• les ſhooe for the foote of a Pigmey: yet all theſe we muſt haue, and all in one play, or tis already condemn'd to the hell of eternall diſgrace. Nay I beſeech you ſir, if you be his friend, ſtand ſo to him ſtill, for he hath too many enemies already, in whoſe judgements, he and his labours ſtand excommunicate, as though unworthy to preſent themſelues in this aſſembly. Either ſee it all or none; for tis growen into a cuſtome at playes, if any one riſe (eſpecially of any faſhionable ſort) about what ſerious buſines ſoever, the reſt thinking it in diſlike of the play, though he never thinks it, cry mew, by • eſus vilde; and leaue the poore heartleſſe children to ſpeake their Epilogue to the empty ſeats. You ſhould not deale gentleman-like with us els.
VVElcome gallants, welcome honor'd bloods; the reaſon that we haue uncloth'd us of our princely government in Arcadia, and haue to doe with this private retire ment here in this deſert Ile, you ſhall find in that ſhedule, only thus much for publicke ſatisfaction: Tis not ſtrange to you, that the choiſeſt treaſure Nature indow'd us with, is min'd up in the veines of my two daughters: how much their quiet, and the ſmooth ſtreame of our government in Arcadia, was troubled by the im petuous concourſe of untruely ſuters, is familiar with your know ledge; this to avoid, I haue for my Image there in my abſence ap pointed my brother, and undertooke this private retirement. To that intent our Iland is fenc't in By ſea and land, and at each corner built A Caſtle for defence, which like great men, Doe over-looke Arcadia: over which, Wee haue appointed Captaines. More to deſire, Is more then we are willing to diſcover. An ague? what ague? If you retaine the loue of children, or the dutie of ſub jects, expreſſe it in your obedience, we know Dametas loues us ▪ In ſigne whereof wee make him. In my free thoughts you wrong him, therefore to ex preſſe our loue, aud to giue the world publicke note of his loyaltie, we create him your Gardian. I minion, yours. Well ſaid Haggart, Ile make your proud heart ſtoope to the lure of obedience. But come, by this time our challenge is pub liſht, and our gallants wits ſweating in the field of Invention, and it behoues us not to reſt unexerciſed. So to our lodge, in the meane time be it knowne, Our breath has power to raiſe, or caſt men downe. Thankes good Dametas, bee thy directions our wiues convoy. Tell me Dametas, was not the Deare a prodigall? did hee not ſpend his breath freely amongſt us? It pleaſeth your modeſty to leſſon it, But it ſhall ſtill liue great in our regard. What woodman's that? What ere he be, he hath deſeru'd our loue, Fellow be neere us, and for this deſert, Perform'd againſt thoſe Traytors to our blood, Vnder thy maſter we giue thee an attendant, To guard the life and ſafetie of our daughter. Truce to this ayrie warre, theſe paper bullets Better become a Cloſſet then a Parke, The Forreſt muſicke is to heare the hounds Rend the thin ayre, and with a luſty cry Awake the drowſie Eccho, and confound Their perfect language in a mingled ſound, Then to the Court, our Forreſt ſport being done, A ſecond chace of lovelier ſports begunne. Zelmane. My thoughts come like a ſaile afore the wind, ſwolne big with news, and thine eares the midwife muſt deliver me of this bur den: my Dutcheſſe is ſicke, heart-ſicke for thee Zelmane. Shall I be ſhort with thee? My Ladie's in love with thee. With thee my Lady: her amorous glances are her accuſers, her very looks write Sonnets in thy commendations, ſhe carves thee at boord, and cannot ſleepe for dreaming on thee in bed, ſhee's turn'd ſunne-riſer, haunts private walkes, and like a diſgrac'd Courtier, ſtu dies the Art of melancholly. Nay never pitty her, ſhe deſerves none, rather lets bend our indeavors to intangle her more. To ſee the kindnes of fortune, who fearing we ſhould be acquainted with ſollitude in this our 12 month retirement, hath begot a domeſticall merriment, and made our own thoughts Actors in't, and as bad a Poet as I am, Ile ha one ſcene in't of my owne invention. Tis ready plotted already, and that the Dutcheſſe may not find thee unprovided when ſhe comes to court thee. Why that's the very happineſſe of the jeſt, but in any caſe confeſſe thy ſelfe a man. Tuſh, Ile furniſh thee, ſay thou art a Prince, no matter who, and haſt to doe with this diſguiſe of purpoſe to court my daughter Violetta. Love durſt not, good, good, excellent, what next? Rare, rare, rare, ſhee's his, ſeald and deliverd in the pre ſence of her husband. Now, what for that now? Excellent vertues in a woman. To ſee an old Dutcheſſe a young Lady kiſſe. Now the plot packs, the ſcene's all comicall, I cannot ſpeake for laughter, to ſee theſe women, That would be counted wonders for their wit, Lay plots to gull themſelves, ſilly conceit. And arme her ſelfe To laugh at me, make jeſts and ſcoffes at me, But ſooth her humour, the revenge ſhee'd throw Vpon my head, ſhall fall on her owne brow.
Why my Lord, are you ſo covetous of your daughters beau ties, that their perfections ſhall bee a meanes to hinder their prefer ment?
Rather to further it faire Queene: they are the only pearles of our age, and to ſee them wel ſet in honourable and well-befitting Marriage, is our wiſhes happineſſe. To which effect we haue ſent a generall challenge To all the youthfull bloods of Affrica, That whoſoever (borne of princely ſtem) Dares foote the boſome of this deſert Ile, (The ſtage where Ile performe this lovers prize) And by his wit and actiue pollicie, Wooe, win, intice, or any way defeate Me of my charge, my daughters of their hearts, Shall with their loues weare my imperiall crowne Wreath of their conqueſt. Here my Gynetia. What meane theſe weapons, are our daughters • afe?
A prize, a prize, rare worke for Fencers. Well then ſiſter, I ſee we muſt to hap-hazard for husbands. Loue an't be thy will, ſend me one with a faire table in his forehead, like Time. Why your quotidian, Dametas the Court ſurfet, hee that dwels in your eye, like a diſeaſe in your blood. He is the moſt miſhapen ſute of gentility that ever the Court wore. Nay, you haue beſtowed too much of the making of him up already. So was the end of ours to liue in peace, And not to tyranniſe on harmeleſſe beaſts, But Forreſters, like Images ſet forth The tyrannie of greatneſſe without pitty, As they the Deare, ſo covetous wealth purſues The trembling ſtate of their inferiors, And to claſpe up the volume of their ſinnes, They drinke their blood, and cloath them with their skins: Then ceaſe to preſſe poore beaſts with tyrannie, You loue your liues, thinke they are loath to dye. For our loues ſiſter, you may ſee, the properer women, the worſe lucke. No at any hand ſiſter, for with a feare it comes. Then let them keepe away ſtill, for I haue vowed my mai denhead ſhall never doe homage to the bed of a coward. Yes faith Dametas. Thanke you good father, who ever looſe by the bargaine, I haue got me a ſervant by the match: woo't ſerue me fellow? Ile try your dutious ſervice: I command Your knee to ki •• e the ground, your lip my hand. Here's hot loue no doubt, I may command my man, and goe without. Woo't beleeve mee ſiſter? I never eat a cherry, but it puts mee in mind of a husband, it kiſſes my lips with ſuch a harmeleſſe prettineſſe. Of what, not of husbands Violetta? Surfet after what, a husband? I warrant you ſiſter, an old Lady in Lacedemon taught me a preſervative againſt that. Marry this it was, ſtill ſaid ſhe, betwixt every cherry ſaid ſhe, be ſure to cracke a ſtone ſaid ſhe. You muſt take heed you cracke not too many too, for you may ſurfet of the ſtone as well as of the cherry. So have I too for this time, but ſiſter, is it not a ſtrange kind of ſervile liberty that we live in here in Arcadia? And for what cauſe forſooth? only to keep us from mariage. By this ſtone, me thinks I long like a woman with child, till I know the difference betwixt a Mayd and a wife. O that I had bin with thee I might ha been ſo too: for the love of marriage how? Is that a creature? And with old women too. In what agreed you? Would I had dreamt I might ha' done ſo too. Otwould ha' vext a Saint, my blood would burne To be ſo neere, and miſſe ſo good a turne. You ſhould not be my ſiſter elſe. And in good earneſt wee are not fath • r • 〈…〉 amiſſe. As of a ſweet Almond in a rugged ſhell, the Sun in a cloud, or a wealthy Diamond in a rocke, indeed cleane contrary to the world, hee weares the worſt ſide outward, and is much better then he ſeemes: but what thinke you of your manly Amazon?? How ever man or woman, the jeſt holds currant in one. You were as ſhe is? but faith madam Mopſa, I perceiue my ſer vant Dorus beares a moneths mind to you, bee not ſo ſtraight laced to him. I meane let fall ſome comforta ble lookes on your ſuter. Why that's kind ly ſaid, and Dorus your loue is very ambitious, to climbe ſo high as the beautifull Mopſa. Theſe extraordinary graces muſt not want admira tion, but where's your mother? Nay, ſhee cannot bee ſaid to ſteale a nap, for the noiſe ſhee makes herſelfe would diſcover her theft: but Dorus ſith your for tunes are poore, you ſhould ſtudy to enoble your deſerts, and beget effects worthy to court and win your Ladies acceptance. What a keenes neceſſitie ſets upon the edge of invention, truſt me Mopſa your ſervant ſpeakes well, and if hee can proue himſelfe the man he ſpeakes of, and my wiſhes well hope, Demetrius, you haue no reaſon to thinke ſcorne of him. I am no counſeller, but ſhould Demetrius in like diſguiſe court me, thus would I embrace him, thus ſeale my affections with a kiſſe, and thus argue: thinke not Demetrius that the clouds of baſe neſſe could ſo muſfle thee, but that the Sun of valour ſhind through them long ſince, and in regard of thy ſerviceable dutie in concealing, and unprevented policy in thus making knowen thy loue, ſort but out fit opportunity, and in deſpight of al guardians ſtrict obſervance, goe where thou wilt, the worth of Demetrius ſhall draw Hippolita, this would I vow, and this will I performe. You were worſe then the devill elſe, for they ſay hee helps his ſervants, then you may doe little and you cannot helpe yours. Yes ſaith Gallants, you have very ſtrange carding and you knew all, but I hope you'l offer up your cards, and yield the ſet loſt. VVhy father, is't not time that we were ſped? Tis a great charge to keep a Mayd ••• -head, Loſe it we muſt, and to prevent ill courſe, Better to giv't, then haue it tane perforce, If you be pleas'd let envy doe her worſt, Spit out her poyſon, or contain't and burſt. VVelcome to all, to all a kind good-night, They truely live, that live in ſcorne of ſpight.
What coward would not venter a crackt crowne for ſuch a bootie? God ſend me one with a good face and I care not. Nay, and his face be good, let me alone to tricke his fore head, a countrey-gentlewoman taught me how: But father I won der how you dare undertake ſuch a peremptory challenge againſt all commers, conſidering you haue beene ſo long troubled with •• Ague. And the Preſence were not exceeding empty-ſtomackt, it would never diſgeſt ſuch Almes-basket-ſcraps, the very fall and gar bidge of gentry; fie upon him, hee becomes the great chamber worſe then a Gentleman-uſher with wry legges. Had hee not beene of my fathers owne making, I ſhould haue condemned his taylor for an exceeding botcher. As Captaines and Courtiers doe old widdowes, for pro fit and preferment. The very making of him up, has ſtood you in more then the whole outſide's worth. How father, my Gardian? Doe you heare father, bid him beſpeake ſpectacles, for my fingers haue vowed to haue a blind match with his eyes. We are your loues debters kind Dametas. As I loue vertue I pitty theſe poore beaſts, Theſe Syl • ane commoners, to ſee what taskes Our covetous Forreſters impoſe upon them, Who not content with impoſt of their breath, (Poore hearts) purſue them ſmiling to their death. And ſome of you too hard-hearted, but leaving this diſ courſe of hunting, haue all our gallantry of Lacedemon and Greece, ſpent the vigor of their wits, that not one dares venter. Then ile feare of purpoſe, becauſe I would haue 'em come. Let your returne be ſpeedy good Dametas. Out of the Court, and the whole Countrey ſhall haue a good riddance. Murther, treaſon, reſcue, helpe. As a thiefe in a mill father, we thanke our redeemers ▪ Now in good deed lo I loue em a liſe too, I thinke I ſhall never ha my belly full on em. No, of cherries Hippolita, but take heed of em, they bee a very filling meat, and dangerous things for us Maydes I can tell you, we may ſurfet after em preſently. I, and after cherries too Hippolita. Then let me alone, Ile cracke a couple of ſtones betwixt e very cherry, rather then ſurfet on them. Nay and they be ſuch dangerous things, I ha done with em. For all the world as Engliſhmen keep their fellons, and Ita lians their wives, we never ſtirre abroad without our laylors. Well, god a mercy of all curſen ſoules, I was neere the know ledge on't laſt night I can tell you. Why thus: As I lay ſlumbring in my bed, No creature with me but my mayden-head. Some maintaine it is, Got in the eye, conceived in a kiſſe; Others, whoſe ſpeech ſeemes neere akin to truth, Say tis a paſſion, bred i'th heat of youth, Some call't a ſigh, and ſome an amorous grone, All differ in the definition: But in th'allow'd opinion of moſt, Tis never truely had till it be loſt. But lying thus alone, as Mayds doe uſe, Me thought I dreamt, as Mayds can hardly chuſe, And in my dreame me thought twas too much wrong A pretty Mayd ſhould lye alone ſo long; With that a gallant comes, gallants can doe Much with young Mayds. He courted me once, and agen, and thrice, Tis vertue to ſay nay, to bee too nice Agrees not with my humour, yet ſome ſay, We Mayds wiſh things, to which we anſwer nay; Briefely, me thought he ſtood ſo long a wooing, I rather could ha wiſht he had been doing Some other buſineſſe, yet at laſt we'greed, Twere ſtrange if earneſt futers ſhould not ſpeed. In our Wedding-ring, Time, place, and houre, indeed in every thing; The day appoynted, and each thing in frame, I thought each houre an age untill it came, Well, come it is, the morning once in ſight, I thought it ten times longer till twas night. At dinner time me thought I ſweld with pride To be drunke to by name of Miſtreſſe bride, Muſicke ſpake loud, no delicates were ſcant, Yet ſtill me thought another thing did want, For ſure thought I, there's ſomething in a man That wiues loue well, hope brides may wiſh it than. Long lookt for comes at laſt, to bed we goe. My bed-mate turn'd, and as he would ha' ſpoke, I ſweat with feare, and in that feare I woke, But ſeeing my kind bed-fellow was gone, Lord how it chaft me that I wakt ſo ſoone, One minuts dreaming longer, I had tride, The difference twixt a virgin and a bride. Are you avis'd of that, and Ifaith tell •… what thinke you of your ſervant Dorus. Lets caſt a choiſe, the neereſt two take one. Come, here's agood. Ile leade. We haue both one mind. In leaving the old folke behind. By the faith a me, well lead. Whither? I am ſure you would not. I hope you would not hurt me, and you ſhould. Soure, ſo I heard you ſay. Of what acquaintance pray? None of my Maydenhead father, I am gone, The Amazon hath wonne one. The caſt I doe. Nay ſcrape out that. Me yours? Much: in my tother hoſe. The leader as the follower. I take your lay. Pardon me mother, Ile beare all or none. Me? Then take your winnings, Ile not die in debt. In earneſt in good truth. In jeſt? Tis the faſhion, Much in requeſt among our nation. Now and then, And being gone, to kiſſe it backe agen: For lovers indentures nere are fairly drawn, Vntill the Maiden-head be left in pawne, As earneſt of the match, ſo mothers ſed, And ſo will daughters doe when mams be dead. Strangers? why father ſtrangers are as welcome to mee, as mine owne Country-men, if they bring good manners and civill hu manity in their company; otherwiſe, they are like foule weather, come afore they be ſent for. Dametas? nay then we ſhall have newes enough, for he ne ver comes into the preſence, but he brings a whole ſacke full of lies, of newes I ſhould ſay.
Now Captaine Obſervation, times bawd, thou that haſt kept the Ages doore, whilſt up-ſtart baſeneſſe crept into the bed of greatneſſe, what doeſt thou thinke of this change? Thats no part of my meaning, yet would I gladly bee better inſtructed why the Duke broke up his Court in Arcadia, and removed it into this Iland. Your words throw ſenſe into me, and thats the cauſe the Iland is ſo ſurely guarded with Watch-towers, over which our ſelues and other Captaines haue the charge. If inquiſitiueneſſe be not too bold a gueſt, what do you thinke of Dametas? Your compariſon holds, for by report, his avarice has unmade many to make him up. As ſome doe upon offices, by fortune and flattery, or as truth ſayes, the Prince having one day loſt his way, wandring in the woods, found this Dametas, affected his diſcourſe, tooke him along to the Court, and like great men in loue with their owne doings, countenanc't his defects, gaue him offices, titles, and all the additi ons that goe to the making up of a man worſhipfull. A paſſing ſtrange curſe, and no queſtion he has travelled farre for ſome of the times. No matter for reaſon, there's rime enough if that be good. Sure hee had ſome reaſon to make this rime, and a man could picke it out. But where's the wag that invited us to this banquet of mirth, ſhrunke in the wetting? That, or ſome knavery elſe upon my life: I had the boy in ſhrewd ſuſpicion at the firſt. Then we are ſped, for in ſuſpitions face I ſee ſome ſubtle ſtratagem in chace.
That it pleas'd the Duke, and becomes not ſubjects to examine his actions. FArewell bright Sunne, thou lightner of all eyes, Thou fall'ſt to give a brighter beame to riſe. Each tree and ſhrub weare trammells of thy haire, But theſe are wiers for none but Kings to weare, And my rude tongue, ſtriving to blaze her forth, Like a bad Arts-man, does diſgrace her worth: But here's the place, upon this Chriſtall ſtreame, Where Citharea did unyoake her teame Of ſiluer Doves to interchange a kiſſe With young Adonis, ſhall I meet my bliſſe? The gentle minutes crown'd with chryſtall flowers, Loſing their youths, are growne up perfect houres, To haſten my delight: The baſhfull Moone, That ſince her dalliance with Endymion Durſt never walke by day, is under ſaile, In ſtead of ſheetes has ſpread her ſilver vaile, Each gliding Brooke and every buſhy tree, Being tipt with ſilver, weare her livery; And the dimme night, to grace our amorous warres, Hath ſtucke nine Spheares full of immortall ſtarres, In ſtead of pearles; the way on which ſhe treads Is ſtrew'd with chryſtall deaw and ſilver beades: Enter Dutcheſſe. She comes, her feet make muſicke with the ground, And the chaſt aire is raviſht with the ſound, My ſoule flies forth to meet her: hell, my wife, Her preſence like a murtherer drives the life Out of my pleaſures breſt, her jealous eye Envies the heaven of my felicity. What makes old Autumne out a bed ſo late? That ſnow ſhould goe a wooing to the Sunne, When one warme kiſſe workes her confuſion! She dogs her ſure, and ſhe to ſhake her off Hath tane ſome other walk, Ile place mine care In diſtance of her will.
